n: Now Naomi takes the initiative. Just as Ruth cared for her, she wants to secure “rest” for Ruth — a safe, settled home through marriage.
Naomi reminds Ruth that Boaz is a relative and tells her he will be at the threshing floor that night, winnowing barley.

f.g: Tosses threshed grain into the evening breeze so the wind blows away the light chaff while the heavier grain falls.
A flat, hard area outside town where grain was processed; owners often slept there at harvest to guard the grain.

n: Naomi tells Ruth to bathe, perfume herself, and put on her best clothing — perhaps signaling the end of her mourning — and to wait until Boaz has finished his meal.
Ruth is to uncover Boaz's feet and lie down there. This was a bold but proper way to make a request; Boaz would then decide what to do.

f.g: A symbolic act asking for his protection and attention; the story treats it as honorable, not immoral (see verse 11).

n: Ruth trusts Naomi completely and agrees to follow her plan.
Ruth goes to the threshing floor and carries out Naomi's instructions exactly.
After a satisfying harvest meal, Boaz settles down to sleep beside the grain pile. Ruth quietly uncovers his feet and lies down.

f.g: He was content and in good spirits after a good harvest and meal.

n: At midnight Boaz wakes with a start — perhaps from the chill on his feet — and discovers a woman lying at his feet.
Ruth identifies herself and boldly asks Boaz to spread his garment over her — a request for marriage — because he is a kinsman-redeemer with the right to help the family.

f.g: “Skirt” is the corner of a garment; the same Hebrew word is “wings.” Ruth asks Boaz to be the answer to his own prayer about God's wings.

n: Boaz blesses Ruth for this second act of loyal love. She could have pursued a younger man, but chose to marry within Naomi's family to preserve its name.
Boaz reassures Ruth and promises to do what she asks. The whole town knows she is a woman of noble character.

f.g: Hebrew ’eshet ḥayil, “a woman of strength/worth” — the same phrase as Proverbs 31, and matching the description of Boaz in Ruth 2:1.

n: But there is a complication: another relative is more closely related and has the first right to act as redeemer.
Boaz promises with an oath that if the nearer relative will not redeem, he will. He asks Ruth to rest until morning, protecting her from traveling home in the dark.

f.g: To act as go'el — redeem the land and marry the widow to raise up the family name.

n: Ruth leaves before dawn, while it is too dark to recognize anyone. Boaz wants to protect her reputation from gossip.

f.g: before it was light enough to recognize faces

n: Boaz fills Ruth's shawl with a generous amount of barley as a gift — a sign of his good faith and a promise of more to come.

f.g: Probably a large shawl or cloak.
The unit is not stated; it was as much as Ruth could carry.

n: Naomi eagerly asks how things went, and Ruth tells her everything Boaz did.

f.g: Probably means “How did it go?” or “What is your situation now?”

n: Ruth reports Boaz's words: he did not want her to return to Naomi empty-handed. This answers Naomi's earlier lament that she came home “empty.”
Naomi tells Ruth to wait patiently; Boaz is a man of his word and will settle the matter that very day.
